Source: (Wood Mackenzie Power & Renewables and Solar Energy Industries Association 2025b; Hryshko et al. 2025; PV Tech Research 2025) Crystalline-Silicon Modules The introduction of new U.S. tariffs since 2018, coupled with federal incentives introduced in 2022, have coincided with many companies investing in the U.S. module supply chain. In 2024, the United States manufactured 7.6 GW of c-Si modules, a 155% increase over 2023, with dc approximately 41 GW of domestic c-Si module assembly capacity operational by the end of dc 2024.1 By the second quarter (Q2) of 2025, an estimated 43 GW of domestic c-Si module dc assembly capacity was operational with an additional 6 GW under construction. Still, most U.S. dc demand in 2024 was met by imports. In 2024, record levels of c-Si modules (56.1 GW ) and dc cells (13.8 GW ) were imported into the United States. The United States imported 89% of c-Si dc modules in 2024 from Vietnam, Thailand, Cambodia, Malaysia, and the remaining countries within the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN). ASEAN (64%) and South Korea (32%) were the source for 96% of c-Si cell imports. Although U.S. trade restrictions have limited cell and module imports directly from China, many PV components and much of the equipment used to make cells and modules are from China. In addition, many Southeast Asian PV manufacturing companies are Chinese controlled. In 2024, the single U.S. c-Si cell manufacturer could serve 2% of U.S. PV modules produced, and there was no domestic wafer production.
